function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL and retrieves data as specified by the parameters. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The URL to which the GET request is sent. It is expected to be a well-formed HTTP or HTTPS URL.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: The Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

headers.description: A dictionary of HTTP headers to send with the request. Each key-value pair represents a header name and its value.

timeout.description: The number of seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up, as a float, or a (connect_timeout, read_timeout) tuple. This is a float type value.

lat.description: Latitude of the location for the query, in degrees. This is a float type value.

lon.description: Longitude of the location for the query, in degrees. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters to append to the URL for the GET request.

allow_redirects.description: Determines if HTTP redirections (301, 302, etc.) should be followed.

auth.description: A tuple representing the user credentials for HTTP authentication, typically in the form of (username, password).

cert.description: Path to an SSL certificate file to verify the peer, or a tuple of (certificate file, key file).

cookies.description: A dictionary of cookies to send with the request. The key is the cookie name and the value is the cookie value.

http.description: URL of the proxy for HTTP requests.

https.description: URL of the proxy for HTTPS requests.

proxies.description: A dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy.

stream.description: If True, the response content will not be downloaded immediately but streamed.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate or not, or a path to a CA bundle if verification is needed.

Below I’ll walk through **what “Startup Stat API” usually means**, outline several popular options you can tap into, and then give you concrete examples (Python snippets + curl commands) so you can start pulling real‑world startup data right away. --- ## 1️⃣ What Do People Usually Want From a “Startup Stat API”? | Metric | Typical Source | |--------|----------------| | Company profile (name, industry, HQ city, founding year) | Crunchbase, AngelList, LinkedIn | | Funding history & valuation rounds | Crunchbase, Pitchbook, CB Insights | | Revenue / ARR estimates | SaaS Capital, PrivCo, Crunchbase | | Employee count & growth | Crunchbase, LinkedIn, Glassdoor | | Market size & TAM | CB Insights, Pitchbook, Owler | | Competitor landscape | SimilarTech, BuiltWith, Crunchbase | If your goal is *“give me a quick snapshot of a company’s health”*, most of those pieces live behind paid feeds—Crunchbase Pro, Pitchbook, CB Insights, etc.—but there are still ways to get useful data at zero cost: * Publicly available datasets (Y Combinator batches, SEC filings) * Free tiers of commercial APIs (AngelList, Crunchbase Basic) * Scraping where legally permissible (e.g., Crunchbase public pages) Below are three practical approaches depending on your budget and technical stack. --- ## 2️⃣ Approach #1 – Use Crunchbase’s Official REST API (Paid Tier Required) > ⚠️ **Note**: Crunchbase requires a subscription for anything beyond the very limited free tier. > You’ll receive an `API_KEY` once you sign up. ### 2a. Quick Setup ```bash pip install requests python-dotenv ``` Create `.env`: ``` CRUNCHBASE_API_KEY=YOUR_CRUNCHBASE_TOKEN_HERE ``` ### 2b. Sample Code (Python) ```python import os from dotenv import load_dotenv import requests load_dotenv() TOKEN = os.getenv("CRUNCHBASE_API_KEY") HEADERS = { "Accept": "application/json", "Authorization": f"Bearer {TOKEN}" } def fetch_company(company_name): """Return basic info + latest funding round.""" url = f"https://api.crunchbase.com/v3.1/entities/{company_name.lower()}/profile" resp = requests.get(url, headers=HEADERS, timeout=10) resp.raise_for_status() data = resp.json()["data"]["organization"] result = { "Name": data["properties"]["short_description"], "Founded": data["properties"].get("founded_on"), "Industry": data["properties"].get("category_code"), "Employees": data["relationships"]["employees"]["items"][0]["total_items"] \ if data["relationships"]["employees"]["items"] else None, "Funding Rounds": [] } # Grab funding rounds fund_url = f"https://api.crunchbase.com/v3.1/organizations/{company_name.lower()}/funding_rounds" r = requests.get(fund_url, headers=HEADERS, params={"page_size": 20}, timeout=10) r.raise_for_status() rounds = r.json().get('data', {}).get('items', []) for rnd in rounds[:5]: # top 5 recent rounds result['Funding Rounds'].append({ "Round Type": rnd["properties"]["round_type"], "Amount USD": rnd["properties"]["raised_amount_usd"], "Date": rnd["properties"]["closed_date"] }) return result if __name__ == "__main__": print(fetch_company("stripe")) ``` #### Expected Output (truncated): ```json { "Name": "Stripe Inc.", "Founded": "2010-12-01", "Industry": "payments", "Employees": 50000, "Funding Rounds": [ {"Round Type":"Series D","Amount USD":650000000,"Date":"2021-07-28"}, ... ] } ``` ### 2c. Curl Example ```bash curl -H "Accept: application/json" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $CRUNCHBASE_API_KEY" \ "https://api.crunchbase.com/v3.1/entities/stripe/profile" ``` --- ## 3️⃣ Approach #2 – Leverage AngelList’s Public GraphQL Endpoint (Free) AngelList offers a lightweight GraphQL interface that lets you pull basic company metadata without paying. No API keys required! ### 3a. Install Dependencies ```bash npm init -y && npm i node-fetch graphql-request ``` ### 3b. Node.js Script (`angel_list_query.mjs`) ```javascript #!/usr/bin/env node import { gql, GraphQLClient } from 'graphql-request'; const client = new GraphQLClient('https://api.angellist.co/graphql'); async function getCompany(slug) { const query = gql` query($slug:String!) { organization(where:{slug:$slug}) { id slug name description websiteUrl foundedAt employeesCount totalRaisedUSD lastFundedAt } } `; try { const variables = { slug }; const res = await client.request(query, variables); console.log(JSON.stringify(res.organization, null, 2)); } catch(err){ console.error('Error:', err.response?.errors || err.message); } } // Replace 'stripe' with whatever org slug you’re interested in await getCompany(process.argv[2] ?? 'stripe'); ``` Run it: ```bash node angel_list_query.mjs stripe ``` Sample output: ```json { "id": "12345", "slug": "stripe", "name": "Stripe", "description": "...", "websiteUrl": "https://stripe.com/", "foundedAt": "2010-09-15T00:00:00Z", "employeesCount": 4000, "totalRaisedUSD": 1100000000, "lastFundedAt": "2021-08-02T00:00:00Z" } ``` ⚡️ **Tip:** For more advanced queries (investor networks, job listings), consult [Angelist’s GraphQL docs](https://docs-angels-list-com.readthedocs.io/en/latest/) — many fields are publicly accessible. --- ## 4️⃣ Approach #3 – Build Your Own Mini‑API Using Public Data Sources Sometimes you don’t have a ready‑made feed, but you do have raw CSV files or web pages. Here’s a minimal Flask app that serves startup stats pulled from a static dataset (e.g., YC Batch 2023). ### 4a. Prepare Dataset Download the YC Batch 2023 spreadsheet → convert to CSV → store locally. Example row schema: | Name | City | Founded | Employees | Valuation | Website | |------|------|---------|-----------|------------| ### 4b. Flask App Skeleton ```python # startup_api.py from flask import Flask, jsonify, abort import csv app = Flask(__name__) DATA_FILE = "./yc_23.csv" @app.route("/startups/", methods=["GET"]) def get_startup(name): with open(DATA_FILE, newline='', encoding='utf8') as f: reader = csv.DictReader(f) for row in reader: if row["Name"].lower() == name.lower(): return jsonify(row) abort(404, description="Startup not found") @app.route("/", methods=["GET"]) def index(): return """

YC 2023 Startup Stats

Use `/startups/<name>` to retrieve a single record.

""" if __name__ == "__main__": app.run(debug=True) ``` Start the service: ```bash export FLASK_APP=startup_api.py flask run --port 8000 ``` Now hit: ```bash curl http://localhost:8000/startups/bloomreach ``` Response: ```json {"Name":"BloomReach","City":"San Francisco","Founded":"2017","Employees":"200+","Valuation":"$300M","Website":"https://www.bloomreach.com"} ``` This approach gives you full control over the data source and eliminates vendor lock‑in—but remember to keep the CSV updated manually or automate ingestion from sources like Crunchbase exports. --- ## 5️⃣ Putting It All Together – A Unified Wrapper If you plan to support multiple providers, wrap each provider in a class and expose a simple unified method: ```python class ProviderBase: def lookup(self, name): raise NotImplementedError() class CrunchbaseProvider(ProviderBase): ... class AngelListProvider(ProviderBase): ... providers = { "crunchbase": CrunchbaseProvider(), "angellist": AngelListProvider(), } def find_startup(provider_key, name): prov = providers.get(provider_key) if not prov: raise ValueError("Unsupported provider") return prov.lookup(name) print(find_startup("angellist", "stripe")) # returns dict ``` That way you can switch between providers based on availability, pricing, or feature set. --- ## 📌 Bottom Line | Option | Cost | Ease of Integration | Key Features | |--------|------|---------------------|--------------| | Crunchbase API | Paid (Pro+) | Very easy (REST) | Full corporate profiles, funding, M&A, market sizing | | AngelList GraphQL | Free | Easy (GraphQL) | Core company data, investors, jobs | | Custom CSV/API | Zero | Medium (requires maintenance) | Tailored data sets, offline analytics | Pick whichever fits your needs and budget. Let me know if you’d like deeper dives into any specific provider, help setting up OAuth flows, or guidance on parsing the returned JSON structures. Happy coding!
